claims.text: High-entropy alloy matrices can retain partial or short-range chemical order at elevated temperatures.
Partial chemical ordering governs the structural stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Partial chemical ordering governs the chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
High configurational entropy maintains partial chemical ordering at elevated temperatures.
Pre-annealing near 600 °C establishes a microstructure with minimal segregation.
Short-range chemical ordering affects grain-boundary migration at elevated temperature.
Short-range chemical ordering affects phase formation at elevated temperature.
High configurational entropy delays large-scale phase separation.
Local ordering of selected elemental pairs reduces grain-boundary mobility.
Local elemental-pair ordering promotes compositional stability.
The combination of high configurational entropy and local ordering increases resistance to high-temperature coarsening.
After repeated high-temperature cycles, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit at least 20–30% less average grain growth than a conventional Ni-based superalloy.
After repeated high-temperature cycles, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less chemical segregation than a conventional Ni-based superalloy.
Strongly negative mixing enthalpy for selected elemental combinations can make short-range ordering insufficient to prevent phase separation.
At sufficiently high service temperatures, short-range ordering can become insufficient to prevent phase separation.
Quantitative measurement of short-range chemical order at high temperature is experimentally challenging.

An otherwise composition-matched state with stronger short-range order should differ in grain growth, segregation, or retained mechanical properties from a lower-order state after identical thermal cycling.
